topics.title: 2016 MathCounts Nationals #21
topics.text:
Manny has 2 red socks, 2 white socks, and 2 blue socks. He plans to choose two socks at random to wear today, two of the remaining socks to wear tommarow, and will the the last two remaining socks the next day. What is the probability that on all three days Manny wears two different colored socks?



I did casework, but didn't get the right answer. Can somebody find my flaw?



He can first choose 2 from the same box, which he can do in 3 ways then again choose two from the same leaving you with 2 cases or he could choose two from a different one in which there is only one case. Here we have 3(2+1)=9.



He could also choose 2 from different boxes which he can do in 3 ways then two from the same where there is only on case or two from different boxes which has 3 cases we have here 3(3+1)=12 cases.



We have a total of 21 cases. For all days to be different we have to have the first one different then the next one different and then the last one is this also different, we already counted this with the 3x3 case so we have 9 cases 9/21=3/7, but this isn't the right answer the correct answer is 8/15.

topics.title: New Mathcounts Prep Book
topics.text:
I've published a workbook, Hard Math for Middle School: Workbook, on Amazon just in time for kids who want last-minute preparation for state mathcounts.



My textbook which has been around for a while (Hard Math for Middle School: IMLEM Plus Edition) has 100+ sections each describing how to solve some type of problems in 1-3 pages. The prose is all about Massachusetts math contests, but it's designed to cover all the math you need for Mathcounts.



The new workbook has 109 worksheets, each with about 6 problems on a section of the text. The problems are labeled by the difficulty level. The L1 problems are designed for kids just starting with contest math. The L2 and L3 problems are like typical and hard mathcounts problems. It gets harder as the book progresses.



I make my books cheaper than most others. The workbook is 8 dollars. The textbook that goes with it is 12. I would get the textbook as well as the workbook -- it explains the math that you should know to do the problems and I've found with my teams that reading about how to do problems is a more efficient way to learn than just doing problems.



Unfortunately, I don't yet have solutions written to all the workbook problems. At some point I'll post them online or try to crowdsource them. But I didn't want to delay the workbook for another year.



Glenn Ellison

topics.title: Confusing Functions
topics.text: $xy=0$ makes the x and y axis on the coordinate plane. It can be written as $y=\frac{0}{x}$ which are two rays similar to horizontal lines along the x-axis starting at (0,0) but never touching (0,0), (sort of like an asymptote), and this value is a function. On the other hand, $x=\frac{0}{y}$ is basically two rays along the y-axis that start at (0,0), but they never touch (0,0), and this is not a function. $xy=0$ goes through (0,0), but dividing it by x or y changes it and instead it does not go through (0,0) anymore. Also, $x=\frac{0}{y}$ is not a function but $y=\frac{0}{x}$ is a function, but those two are the same. This is so confusing... is $xy=0$ a function or not?

topics.title: AMC 10A 2017 #15
topics.text:
This was from this year's AMC 10 test:



Chloé chooses a real number uniformly at random from the interval $[0, 2017]$. Independently, Laurent cooses a real number uniformly at random from the interval $[0, 4034]$. What is the probability that Laurent's number is greater than Chloé's number?



$\mathrm{\textbf{(A)} \ }\frac{1}{2}\qquad \mathrm{\textbf{(B)} \ } \frac{2}{3}\qquad \mathrm{\textbf{(C)} \ } \frac{3}{4}\qquad \mathrm{\textbf{(D)} \ } \frac{5}{6}\qquad \mathrm{\textbf{(E)} \ }\frac{7}{8}$



Why is my solutionNote that there are 2018 numbers that Chloé can choose from and 4035 numbers that Laurent can choose from.

Case 1: Chloé chooses 0

This occurs in a $\frac{1}{2018}$ chance. In order for Laurent's number to be greater, she has to choose from 1...4034 inclusive, which occurs in $\frac{4034}{4035}$ chance.



Case 2: Chloé chooses 1

Similarly, this occurs with probability $\frac{1}{2018} \cdot \frac{4033}{4035}$



...

Case 2018: Chloé chooses 2017

This occurs with probability $\frac{1}{2018} \cdot \frac{2018}{4035}$.



Adding all these cases up, we get $\frac{2018 + 2019 +...+4034}{2018\cdot 4035} = \boxed{\frac{3026 \cdot 2017}{2018\cdot 4035}}$.
 not correct?

topics.title: AMC 10 Problem
topics.text:
Here is a problem from the AMC 10A 2011:



Two counterfeit coins of equal weight are mixed with $8$ identical genuine coins. The weight of each of the counterfeit coins is different from the weight of each of the genuine coins. A pair of coins is selected at random without replacement from the $10$ coins. A second pair is selected at random without replacement from the remaining $8$ coins. The combined weight of the first pair is equal to the combined weight of the second pair. What is the probability that all $4$ selected coins are genuine?



$\textbf{(A)}\ \frac{7}{11}\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{9}{13}\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ \frac{11}{15}\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ \frac{15}{19}\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ \frac{15}{16}$



I don't understand what is wrong with my solutionEach pair must either consist of both genuine or both being 1 genuine and 1 fake



Case 1: Each pair has 2 genuine coins.

There are 8 genuine coins to choose from, so the first pair has $\binom{8}{2}$ ways, and the second pair has $\binom{6}{2}$ ways to choose(since there are 6 coins left). Therefore, there are $\binom{8}{2}\binom{6}{2}$ ways for this case.



Case 2: Each pair has 1 fake and 1 real.

There are $\binom{2}{1}$ ways to choose the fake coin of the first pair and $\binom{8}{1}$ ways to choose the real coin of the first pair. Then there is $\binom{1}{1}$ way to choose the remaining fake coin and $\binom{7}{1}$ ways to choose the real coin of the second pair. Therefore, this case has $\binom{2}{1}\binom{8}{1}\binom{1}{1}\binom{7}{1}$.



Thus, the answer is $\frac{\binom{8}{2}\binom{6}{2}}{\binom{8}{2}\binom{6}{2}+\binom{2}{1}\binom{8}{1}\binom{1}{1}\binom{7}{1}} = \boxed{\frac{105}{133}}$
